L'homme fort d'une "banque de l'IA"

A court terme, ce retour est peut-être une bonne nouvelle. Mais cela montre à quel point Nvidia dépend d'un seul homme. A la fois pour la technologie qu’elle développe, mais aussi pour le réseau et les liens que Jensen Huang a créés autour de Nvidia.

L'entreprise mêle des ventes de puces en échange de prêts ou d'investissements dans des entreprises de la tech. Ce n'est pas pour rien qu'on parle de Nvidia comme de la banque de l'intelligence artificielle: tout l'écosystème tourne autour de cette entreprise devenue gigantesque, et surtout de son patron, maître de ces "deals" (ces accords).

On peut d'ailleurs continuer l'analogie avec les grandes banques dont on dit qu'elles sont "too big to fail" (trop grandes pour faire faillite). Nvidia, sans son directeur emblématique, ne semble pas pouvoir fonctionner. Sans lui, c'est toute la tech qui vacille, peu importe l'éthique. A long terme, donc, ce n'est pas du tout rassurant.
Sujets radio: Mathilde Farine et Loubna Anaki
Adaptation web: Julie Liardet
"C'est très surprenant"

Jensen Huang "revient pour rassurer les marchés. Il revient aussi dans un but politique américain et probablement pour continuer à soutenir le secteur technologique en général", analyse dans La Matinale Julien Leegenhoek, spécialiste de la tech et associé chez Taranis, une société d’investissement basée à Genève.
Mais "tout s'est inversé tout d'un coup. C'est très surprenant", estime aussi le spécialiste, après "la volte-face" du conseil d'administration.

Cette affaire "devient une affaire politique", observe aussi Julien Leegenhoek. Pour lui, "c'est un petit peu à l'image de ce régime américain du moment, où il y a une politisation et une polarisation sur un nombre de sujets croissant".
Donald Trump a joué un rôle clé et des élus américains critiquent

Donald Trump a joué un rôle clé dans le retour de Jensen Huang. Le président américain ne cache pas être intervenu auprès du conseil d’administration de la société. Ce revirement fait beaucoup réagir la classe politique.

Donald Trump l’assure, son parti partage sa position. "Perdre un tel talent serait une honte pour notre pays", selon lui. Mais en réalité, de nombreux élus républicains se sont montrés sceptiques et ont vivement critiqué la décision du conseil d’administration de Nvidia. Tous ont mis en doute les affirmations de la Maison Blanche selon lesquelles il n’y avait pas de risques pour la sécurité nationale des Etats-Unis.
Le sénateur Tom Cotton a affirmé que le Congrès avait encore beaucoup de choses à examiner et que cette affaire n’était "que la partie visible de l’iceberg".

Certains démocrates, comme le sénateur Ruben Gallego, vont jusqu’à accuser la Maison Blanche de corruption. Ils promettent de poursuivre les investigations autour de cette affaire une fois qu’ils auront repris le contrôle des deux chambres du Congrès en janvier.

Donald Trump aurait gagné jusqu'à 15 millions de dollars grâce aux actions Nvidia après le retour de Jensen Huang, selon un article du New York Times. Ces actions avaient chuté ces dernières semaines.

items.titel: Chaud dedans : comment conserver la chaleur du corps en période de crise énergétique
items.anriss: Notre corps est capable de s’adapter et de trouver des ressources pour résister au froid et maintenir sa température… À condition que l’exposition à des températures glaciales ne dure pas trop longtemps.

absaetze.t: [Cet article vous est exceptionnellement proposé en accès libre. Il a été publié le 4 décembre 2022 et republié le 24 novembre 2026.]

Comme les autres mammifères et les oiseaux, nous sommes endothermes. Nous nous servons de la thermorégulation pour maintenir une température constante à l’intérieur de notre corps – entre 37 °C et 37,5 °C. Que l’environnement extérieur change, et s’enclenche alors “tout un éventail de réponses physiologiques, dont la réduction de la température des tissus – la peau, le sang et les muscles”, explique Joseph Costello, spécialiste en physiologie sportive et environnementale au laboratoire de recherche sur les environnements extrêmes à l’université de Portsmouth [dans le sud de l’Angleterre]. “Si l’exposition [au froid] se prolonge dans le temps, on observe également une diminution de la température interne du corps.”

La thermorégulation est gérée par l’hypothalamus, une structure du cerveau profond qui assure notre équilibre interne – l’homéostasie – en régulant certains mécanismes, comme le rythme cardiaque et la température corporelle. Si l’hypothalamus perçoit un refroidissement du corps, il envoie des signaux à la peau, aux glandes, aux muscles et aux organes, déclenchant de leur part des réactions qui permettront à l’organisme de rester chaud et de protéger ses organes vitaux.

Lorsque le corps se refroidit, la priorité est de protéger les organes internes. Si la température extérieure chute à 15 °C, les vaisseaux sanguins proches de la peau se contractent. Le flux sanguin se redirige alors des extrémités – les mains, les pieds, les bras, les jambes et les couches supérieures de l’épiderme – vers l’intérieur de l’organisme afin de maintenir les organes au chaud et ainsi de les protéger.
Climatiques
Chaque jeudi, les pistes de la presse étrangère pour agir face au dérèglement climatique et s’adapter
Chair de poule

La sensation de froid commence par la peau. Certaines personnes y sont plus sensibles que d’autres, en particulier les femmes, les personnes âgées et les enfants en bas âge. Les femmes possèdent plus de tissu adipeux que les hommes : une épaisse couche de graisse sous-cutanée isole les organes internes mais bloque le flux de sang chaud vers la peau et les extrémités. En règle générale, elles possèdent également moins de muscles qui permettent la production de chaleur par les tremblements. Le fait d’avoir moins de muscles ralentit aussi le métabolisme de base – soit la capacité à brûler l’énergie issue de la nourriture.

Chez les personnes âgées, le corps a plus de mal à envoyer le sang vers les endroits qui en ont besoin car le métabolisme ralentit avec l’âge. Quant aux bébés, explique Chris Dewhurst, néonatalogiste à la Women’s NHS Foundation [Fondation pour la santé des femmes] de Liverpool, ils n’ont pas de mécanismes métaboliques aussi développés pour réagir au stress thermique. “Par exemple, les bébés ne tremblent pas, révèle-t-il. Ils ont également un ratio surface de peau-masse corporelle élevé, ce qui veut dire qu’ils se refroidissent plus facilement.” En revanche, les bébés ont du tissu adipeux brun – le même type de graisse que les animaux hibernants. “La graisse brune produit de la chaleur en puisant dans les calories, poursuit Chris Dewhurst. Des calories qui, en temps normal, seraient utilisées pour développer les tissus musculaires et cérébraux.”

Le fait d’utiliser des calories pour conserver la chaleur, précise-t-il, se ressent sur la croissance et le développement du cerveau. Lorsque la température du corps chute, la tension artérielle se met à grimper sous l’effet du volume de sang accru pompé à travers un petit espace. Afin de réduire ce volume de liquide et la tension artérielle, les reins interviennent en filtrant les liquides en excès dans le sang, ce qui conduit la personne à uriner plus souvent. C’est ce qu’on appelle la “diurèse due au froid”. La raréfaction du sang dans l’épiderme peut entraîner un bleuissement lorsque la température de la peau chute sous l’effet du froid. Lorsque le corps est exposé longtemps au froid, cette stratégie de protection peut réduire le flux sanguin dans certaines parties du corps à des niveaux potentiellement dangereux.
Sacrifices et tremblements

À ce stade, le corps peut prendre la décision de risquer de sacrifier les parties dont il a le moins besoin – les doigts, les orteils, les oreilles, le nez, les joues – pour maintenir sa température interne. Lorsque la température de la peau descend à −2 °C, les tissus commencent à geler. À mesure qu’elle gèle, la peau prend une teinte cireuse, pique ou picote, puis s’engourdit. C’est ensuite au tour des tissus profonds de geler. Ce sont les engelures. La peau bleuit, grise ou noircit. À −4 °C, des cristaux de glace se forment dans le sang. En cas d’engelure sévère, la peau devient dure comme du bois. Les muscles et les os commencent à geler à leur tour.

Lorsque le corps n’est plus en mesure de maintenir sa température interne en rétractant les vaisseaux sanguins, il se met à trembler pour augmenter la production de chaleur : les muscles squelettiques se contractent. C’est le premier symptôme de l’hypothermie, qui affecte tous les mécanismes du corps – le métabolisme, l’acuité mentale, la conduction nerveuse, le temps de réaction neuromusculaire, ainsi que les appareils cardiovasculaire et respiratoire. À mesure que la température du corps descend, le sujet éprouve plus de difficultés à articuler, à coordonner ses mouvements et à faire fonctionner sa mémoire. À 32 °C [de température interne], le tremblement cesse. En deçà de 30 °C, les battements du cœur se font irréguliers, la fonction rénale est perturbée, des liquides s’accumulent dans les tissus et les espaces vides des poumons. À 29 °C, on risque la perte de connaissance ; et à 26 °C, la mort.
Des conséquences à long terme

Qu’en est-il lorsque vous êtes exposé à un froid modéré de manière prolongée – par exemple, lorsque vous ne pouvez pas vous chauffer chez vous ? “Exposé à un froid moins intense pendant une longue durée, l’organisme va subir ce qu’on appelle des ‘lésions sans gel des tissus’”, explique Clare Eglin, collègue de Joseph Costello également spécialiste en physiologie environnementale. “Parmi les symptômes d’une lésion sans gel des tissus, on trouve une altération des fonctions sensorielles, une sensibilité au froid et des douleurs liées aux atteintes sur les vaisseaux sanguins et les nerfs des pieds et des mains. Dans certains cas graves, ces symptômes peuvent durer des mois.”

Le fait de respirer de l’air froid sur une longue durée peut irriter les voies respiratoires et les poumons – même chez les sujets sains – et aggraver des problèmes respiratoires existants comme l’asthme, la bronchite ou une pneumopathie chronique obstructive. Quand vous inspirez, le nez et la bouche réchauffent et humidifient l’air avant qu’il n’atteigne les poumons. Lorsque l’air est froid, les voies respiratoires supérieures réagissent en se contractant, rendant la respiration difficile. Par ailleurs, l’air froid contient moins d’humidité que l’air chaud, de sorte qu’il peut provoquer un assèchement des voies respiratoires. “Les infections respiratoires profitent des températures basses”, rappelle Erika Radford, responsable du conseil médical à [l’association d’aide aux victimes de troubles respiratoires] Asthma + Lung UK. “L’hiver est déjà une saison à haut risque pour les gens qui souffrent de pneumopathies, et la pire des choses qui puisse arriver, c’est un déferlement dans les hôpitaux de patients qui ont du mal à respirer en raison d’une exposition au froid.”
Chaud dedans
Il existe certaines méthodes scientifiquement prouvées pour conserver la chaleur du corps – et quelques remèdes de grand-mère à éviter…

Porter un bonnet : les scientifiques ont établi que nous perdions plus de chaleur par le corps que par la tête. Pour autant, il reste utile de porter un bonnet parce que, quand le corps est chaud mais que la tête est froide, on ne tremble pas, ce qui entraîne une chute rapide de la température interne.

Accumuler les couches : le fait d’accumuler les couches fines pour emprisonner l’air reproduit le phénomène d’horripilation, plus connu sous le nom de “chair de poule”, dont profitent souvent les animaux lorsque l’air se trouve emprisonné entre les poils qui se dressent sous l’effet de la contraction des tout petits muscles arrecteurs du poil, situés à la base de chaque follicule pileux.

S’activer : l’activité physique entraîne une contraction des muscles en puisant dans les nutriments, ce qui produit de la chaleur. Le simple fait de monter et descendre une marche peut produire 200 watts de chaleur supplémentaires et faire grimper rapidement la température du corps. Mais n’en faites pas trop ! Si vous surchauffez votre corps et que vous commencez à transpirer, l’évaporation de cette sueur peut se solder par une perte rapide de chaleur.

Éviter l’alcool : il fait affluer le sang à la surface de la peau et l’éloigne ainsi de l’intérieur de l’organisme, faisant chuter la température interne et accroissant donc le risque d’hypothermie. Il est également prouvé que l’alcool entrave le tremblement naturel ainsi que la sensation de froid.

Selon les spécialistes de l’University College de Londres (UCL), des milliers de personnes vont mourir et des millions d’enfants souffrir cet hiver en raison d’une précarité énergétique qui atteint un “niveau épidémique”. “On est en terra incognita”, résume Tammy Boyce, chercheuse associée principale à l’UCL et coautrice du rapport Marmot [sur les inégalités de santé en Angleterre, publié en 2010 et réactualisé en 2020].
“Des maisons qui n’étaient pas froides auparavant vont l’être pour la première fois. Des gens qui n’avaient jamais souffert de précarité énergétique vont en faire l’expérience.”

Les handicapés, les personnes âgées et les enfants seront touchés de plein fouet, ajoute-t-elle, et les effets seront visibles partout, y compris sur les résultats scolaires, la santé mentale et la condition physique. “La seule bonne nouvelle, conclut Tammy Boyce, c’est que les gens vont se rendre compte des effets du logement sur la santé.”

items.titel: Iran orders Hormuz closed 'further day by day' as Qatar seeks to revive peace talks
items.anriss: The IRGC claimed three tankers hit mines in the crucial strait while under US escort, which the Joint Maritime Information Centre said was unconfirmed, as Qatar's prime minister pressed Rubio and Vance to restart talks.

absaetze.t: Iran's army commander-in-chief ordered his navy on Monday to close the Strait of Hormuz "further day by day" until Washington meets Tehran's conditions, warning that any new US military action would draw blows that were "more severe, more crushing and without geographical limitation."
ADVERTISEMENT

"Until the seven conditions of the Islamic Republic of Iran are fulfilled, not only will the Strait of Hormuz not be opened, it must be closed further day by day, conditions for the enemy must become more difficult, and stronger control will be exercised over it," Major General Amir Hatami said, addressing senior commanders of Iran's armed forces.

Citing orders from Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, Hatami added that if the US "commits a new folly and starts another war, in the new phase the blows will be more severe, more crushing and without geographical limitation."
The elite paramilitary IRGC said on Monday that three oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz suffered "powerful explosions and massive fires" after hitting naval mines.
One tanker was hit off the southern shores and two more in the east of the strait, "while under extensive air escort by the US army," an IRGC statement said.
The IRGC said it would publish images of the explosions and warned shipowners that "military escort by the US army is no substitute for compliance with maritime regulations."

The Joint Maritime Information Centre (JMIC), in a report covering 19 to 21 November, said it recorded 114 passages through the strait "with the assistance of the United States" and that claims of tankers hitting naval mines were unconfirmed.

Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Washington was seeking to impose a neither-war-nor-peace situation on Tehran, threatening there were "military ways to break the blockade that, God willing, we will pursue in the near future."
As head of the Iranian delegation in the Islamabad talks, Ghalibaf said there would be no further negotiations or action before Washington moved.

"Before the implementation of Iran's seven conditions there will be no action and no negotiation, and in response to the enemy's moves we are also ready to give a decisive answer and to change the geography of the battlefield in the event of an enemy mistake," Ghalibaf said.

Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told reporters a naval blockade was "tantamount to military aggression" and that Iran had "the right in this regard to use any available means to defend itself."
"We will certainly not tolerate this situation, and we will use all our tools to confront this US aggression," he said.
Qatar wants both sides at the table

Qatar's Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani visited Washington on Monday and met US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President JD Vance to discuss efforts to restart negotiations between Tehran and Washington.
After his talks with Rubio, Al Thani said the region "cannot bear a renewed escalation of tensions between the United States and Iran" and that Doha was working to bring both sides back to the table.
Qatar and the US were also seeking to strengthen their military cooperation, he said. According to AP, citing a source familiar with the proceedings, the meeting with Vance lasted about 10 minutes.

The visit followed US President Donald Trump's statement on Sunday that military strikes on Iran could resume after the New Year. Trump had said earlier this month that he had asked Vance to shift his focus from Iran to domestic policy.

In recent days, Iran has attacked US military bases in Bahrain and Kuwait on several occasions, and Tehran's armed forces have reported almost daily that tankers it describes as violators have struck naval mines.
Qatar hosts the largest US military base in the Middle East and the regional headquarters of CENTCOM, and plays a key mediation role between Tehran and Washington.

items.titel: The Game Is the Easy Part: Measuring Military Strategic Judgment
items.anriss: If a colonel and a Navy captain made the same decisions for the same reasons in a graded wargame, would they get the same score? This question stopped being an academic thought experiment on Nov. 9, 2026. Speaking at the Naval War College, …

absaetze.t: If a colonel and a Navy captain made the same decisions for the same reasons in a graded wargame, would they get the same score?

This question stopped being an academic thought experiment on Nov. 9, 2026. Speaking at the Naval War College, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that “competitive [AI] assisted wargaming and high-stress decision forcing scenarios” would become the “centerpiece of senior officer evaluation.” Further, “these exercises [would] feed directly” into the newly established joint warfighter evaluations: the new assessments for colonels and captains competing for their first star. A memorandum issued the same day directs every staff and war college to establish a “rigorous, standardized culminating capstone wargame or comprehensive exam … to support talent management and stratification decisions.” Despite historical precedents, that is a great deal to ask of a wargame, which is no longer restricted to exploring a problem or teaching a lesson, but will be used to rank people. This is a departure from how they are typically used today in the department.

A test with such high stakes should meet three standards. First, it measures what matters for leaders at this level, rather than how well-suited an officer’s experience happens to be for a specific scenario. Second, it gives the same grade for the same performance, no matter who grades it or how many times. Third, because these officers will compete for joint positions, a grade earned in one service’s evaluation should mean the same thing as another’s.

In other words, the wargaming tests should be valid, repeatable, and comparable. The wargaming field itself has long held that its games produce insight, not measurement, and there is little published evidence that a wargame can meet these criteria despite decades of experience. The memo from the secretary directed a framework to accomplish this in 180 days.

The required scale and frequency to reach proficiency at the format and content in varying contexts make this harder. Officers will be graded on judgment in these games, which can only be built through repeated practice with feedback over years. Expanding the use of AI assessments is a requirement to make this work, but a machine’s feedback is only useful if it can be trusted.

I believe it can be done, and I have spent the past year working on this problem set. I write this as the founder of WarPaths, a platform that grades and assesses individual wargame play. As such, I have an interest in defense contracting for AI usage in the classroom. The first AI-enabled grader I built failed multiple tests I assumed it would pass. I found that the game itself is the easy part and the details of the assessment are the hard part. Delivering the valid, repeatable, and comparable wargaming tests at the necessary scale creates a unique set of challenges.

The memorandum’s specified tasks are straightforward. The military departments should build the capstone and deliver a “standardized assessment and grading framework within 180 days.” Most of the officers’ grades are to come from “objective evaluations such as wargames, planning exercises, strategic essays, and decision-forcing cases.” Critically, the first directive in the memorandum requires that institutional program learning objectives focus on “comprehensive understanding across all domains of warfare.” Service-centric games and evaluation approaches will not suffice.

The memorandum’s implied tasks for wargaming are much more difficult. First, deciding what to measure is the necessary starting point. How much of the grade or assessment is attached to game outcomes versus the reasoning behind the decisions? How is the right balance achieved between strategic reasoning and operational effectiveness? Both play a role in the secretary’s speech and memo.

Second, stakeholders should demonstrate that grading of the tests consistently produces enough distribution to reliably stratify participants — one of the secretary’s requirements — into performance bands. Without this consistent stratification, the intended outcomes of the memo cannot be achieved: Boards would not be able to reliably distinguish good performances from outstanding ones.

Third, this should work at the required scale and frequency. Scale is the number of officers assessed individually. Frequency is how often each should practice, with feedback, to build the judgment being tested. Both are beyond what instructors can do by hand.

The wargaming community largely holds that games as they are typically utilized in the Department of Defense resist quantification. The chair of the Naval War College’s War Gaming Department and two colleagues argued on this site just last year that asking wargames for quantitative precision misunderstands the method. A further complicating factor is the nature of how games are normally built, which is well set in practice. Designed to facilitate discussion, games are built around specific learning objectives with the participants in mind.

So, the wargaming field’s product is typically collective, bespoke, qualitative, and used to learn. The directives require a product that is individual, standardized, objective, comparable across institutions, and used to rank.
The field is correct in that a game cannot measure the war. The question the secretary’s memo raises is: Can a game measure the warfighter, and if so, what are the requirements?

To test these skills fairly requires prolonged practice. But giving every staff and war college student multiple graded scenarios beginning years before the war college is beyond what instructors can do by hand. This is the promise of AI-powered wargames, which can provide the sets and reps needed to build this judgment. But each of those reps should be repeatable — graded the same— or the eventual test is unfair.

Let’s return to the colonel and the Navy captain on the issue of comparability. There are six versions of the Joint Warfighter Evaluation — one for each service and one run by the Joint Staff — and they differ widely in format, though some are still in development. These officers will compete for the same joint billets on different tests, even though the evaluations will only be one data point of many considered by promotion boards.

However, making different tests comparable is established practice. Keys include equal rigor and a common set of assumptions and goals for the tests. The Army has already run a standardized, high-stakes assessment of officers. Its command assessment program began in 2019 with candidates for command, described in these pages at its launch. Until it was canceled in 2025, it put candidates through cognitive and noncognitive tests, a written assessment, a psychologist’s interview, and a double-blind panel interview. The department does not have to start from scratch, but it does need to establish common foundations.
Yet the needed scale and frequency leave no alternative to automated assessments of an officer’s reasoning. This is where the real trouble starts.

The requirements for scoring — automated, delivered on responses to free text inputs, and anchored on a consistent performance standard — logically lead to giving a large language model the transcript, a rubric, and a request for a score. I did that at first with an early wargame scenario. The same play, graded four times, came back 12 points apart on a 100-point scale. A deliberately novice player scored unreasonably high. When I took a strong playthrough and removed its risk reasoning, the risk grade barely moved. The grader credited the player with addressing issues that appeared only in the question.

Built to be helpful, the large language model delivered scores that were artificially inflated and lacked reliable stratification. In response, I improved the constraints on the rubric and varied approaches to distinguish between parts of the questions and answers. Performance only worsened. My experience was consistent with research on AI graders.

One study calls it “rating roulette,” while another found different scores for identical inputs were a common occurrence. Large language models tend to be biased when used as graders: skewed score distributions, a pull toward round numbers, and early attributes’ scores tending to anchor later attributes’ assessments. The necessity to evaluate multiple dimensions of wargame reasoning makes the grading even more problematic: The rubric approach is challenged to support pluralistic criteria.

RAND found large language model judges suffer from bias, low robustness, and misalignment with experts — especially in specialized domains. Rubric engineering cannot solve this. Although RAND did find that the judge could match nonexpert humans on deliberately simple assessments, this is very different from what is required for wargaming.

To understand how grading can work with a large language model, there are a few key concepts. The success criteria we are measuring against is what a human evaluator, guided by a rubric, might rate the performance — not simply consistency across large language model runs. We should also consider the number of dimensions assessed and establish the levels each dimension is assessed on — e.g., a 0-100 or 0-5 scale.

The above-mentioned changes that failed to improve the grader tightened the instructions but still left the large language model to form an overall impression of play and assign a grade to match. Principles that narrowed the performance/expert assessment gap on my platform were to: separate feedback, citation of evidence, and grading into distinct functions; articulate evidence standards at each level of the evaluated dimension; require citation of evidence; and use a quantity of performance levels that match large language model strengths. These helped remove the model’s tendency to assign grades based on impressions and instead rely more on evidence.

A large-language-model-powered grader should pass six tests, the first grouping of which addresses validity. First, a set of tests graded by a model approximates the hand-graded scores assigned by an expert evaluator — guided by a rubric — within an acceptable tolerance level. Second, a planted defect — removal of a key element required from the rubric — results in a predictable drop in score in otherwise identical runs. Third, the addition of extraneous explanatory text — such as buzzwords — does not result in a higher score in otherwise identical runs.

A second grouping addresses repeatability and comparability. Fourth, multiple runs of grading the same transcript result in similar scores within a sufficiently narrow tolerance. Fifth, a grader tuned on one scenario should be checked on scenarios it has never seen — it shows it consistently applies the assessment standards and not its understanding of a scenario. Sixth, updating of the underlying model does not result in different scores for the same set of tests.

items.titel: 'Prendre forme' d'Odile Cornuz, une amie qui vous veut du lien

absaetze.t: Dans son troisième roman, 'Prendre forme', l'autrice neuchâteloise Odile Cornuz explore de façon joueuse le quotidien de Mélusine, une jeune femme qui décide, pour vivre une expérience transformatrice, d'inviter des inconnus à se confier à elle, le temps d'un unique entretien.

Comme le renard du Petit Prince, Mélusine souhaite créer des liens. Mais comment s’y prendre, lorsqu’on est d’un naturel solitaire, et que les cendres d’un amour déçu fument encore? Rencontrer les autres sans y laisser trop de plumes, tel est son désir. La jeune femme rédige donc une petite annonce, proposant à des inconnus de se confier à elle, le temps d’une unique entrevue dédiée au thème du lien.

Avec 'Prendre forme', son troisième roman, Odile Cornuz poursuit son exploration des petites et grandes transformations que la vie dispose sur notre chemin. Autrice de théâtre, poétesse et scénariste, la Neuchâteloise a fait du dialogue le cœur battant de son œuvre romanesque. Dans 'Fusil', en 2022, elle examinait par le truchement des objets l’implacable dissolution d’un couple. Avec 'Qui n’est plus', deux ans plus tard, l’autrice mettait en scène le dialogue singulier d’un fils se confiant au corps mort de son père.

Le dialogue, la parole suscitée par l’échange oral, m’ont toujours fascinée. Entendre le dialogue entre deux personnes, dans les transports publics par exemple, est une manière d’entrer de manière informelle dans leur vie.
Une foule d'inconnus à sa porte

La protagoniste de 'Prendre forme', elle, décide de provoquer le destin. Le récit se présente ainsi sous la forme d’une alternance entre des chapitres consacrés à ces rencontres impromptues et des moments d’introspection, où Mélusine s’interroge sur le bien-fondé de sa démarche. Attirés par cette proposition gratuite, de nombreux inconnus se pressent à sa porte: défilent ainsi, comme au théâtre, des personnages variés, du type agressif qui part furibard à celui qui vient parler de sa mère, d’une femme à la sexualité florissante au culturiste mal dans sa peau.

A chacun son élocution, son humeur, ses marottes. Dans cette société miniature qu’Odile Cornuz convoque, toutes et tous s'interrogent sur la nature de leurs liens, chaînes, laisses ou tendres attaches qui donnent du prix à l’existence. Pour tenir à distance respectable ces confessions insistantes, Mélusine a conçu un jeu. Une série de poèmes imprimés sur de petites cartes, déclinant une série d’actions à l’infinitif: "Espérer une présence", "Craindre le banal", "User du rêve comme un onguent", etc. En guise d’ordonnance, les "patients" de Mélusine héritent ainsi d’une petite carte.

Cherche-t-elle l’amour? Elle n’y croit plus! Elle a été touchée par des récits, voire des confidences. Des brèches de paroles ont ouvert les possibles d’un espace vital, agrandi l’expérience des autres autant que la sienne.
Des poèmes destinés aux lectrices et lecteurs

Joueuse elle aussi, Odile Cornuz ne se contente pas de glisser ces poèmes au fil du roman. A la fin du livre, une série de pages d’un grammage différent propose aux lectrices et lecteurs de découper les cartes de ces poèmes afin de se livrer à leur tour à ce jeu consistant, dans l’esprit du lien, à trouver des manières personnelles d’en conjuguer les verbes.

Le stratagème, pourtant, ne prémunit pas totalement Mélusine contre l’accident heureux. Au fil des rencontres se développent quelques liens plus solides, qui invitent la jeune femme à repenser son rapport à l’amitié ou à la famille. Expérience littéraire et conte moral, 'Prendre forme' dit ainsi avec subtilité comment la circulation des mots peut être, à notre insu, le ferment de profondes métamorphoses.
Nicolas Julliard/mh
Odile Cornuz, 'Prendre forme', éditions Le Verre ardent, novembre 2026

items.titel: Biscuit-tin lids, horse brasses and scrap metal form sculptural V&A Christmas tree by Burberry
items.anriss: Fashion brand Burberry 's chief creative officer Daniel Lee worked with artist Ann Carrington to create a Christmas tree sculpture for the Victoria & Albert Museum , made from "memories, traditions and little treasures."

absaetze.t: Fashion brand Burberry‘s chief creative officer Daniel Lee worked with artist Ann Carrington to create a Christmas tree sculpture for the Victoria & Albert Museum, made from “memories, traditions and little treasures.”

The 16-foot (4.8-metre) tree, which was unveiled this week, sits in the entrance hall of the Victoria & Albert Museum (VA’s) South Kensington location and was designed to celebrate craft and creativity.

“This collaboration with Ann is a celebration of creativity and what better place to showcase this than the V&A?” Lee said. “It’s one of my favourite museums and a constant source of inspiration to me.”

Lee and Carrington made the tree from old money boxes, biscuit and sweet-tin lids, trinket dishes, silver trays, horse brasses and embossed plates, which were turned into rosettes and ribbons and attached to a metal frame.
The tree, which was made as part of Burberry‘s 170th anniversary celebrations, also features ribbons and bows made of scrap metal.
According to Lee, he and Carrington made the sculpture from “memories, traditions and little treasures. Objects and materials that most people would overlook.”
Carrington added that the design was inspired by the ritual of getting old Christmas decorations out of storage in time for the festive season.

“We wanted to capture that magical moment when you retrieve the battered old box of Christmas decorations from the loft, sift through the faded party bows and tattered tinsel accumulated through the generations and begin the joyful ritual of dressing the tree,” she said.
“I’m always drawn to work that’s handmade, and Ann is a master of her craft,” Lee said of the collaboration.

As well as the tree, the V&A will also be showing The Burberry Trench: Crafting an Icon, a display that traces the history of the trench coat. Burberry has a multi-year partnership with the museum and is set to open The Burberry Gallery at the South Kensington location in 2028.
Lee has previously unveiled an archive-inspired logo for Burberry, and a few years ago, the brand revealed its redesigned London flagship store.

items.titel: Exhibition celebrates Delftware, the Dutch art form that became the ‘Ikea of its day’
items.anriss: Show in The Hague looks at the craft, creativity and global influences behind the Netherlands’ best-known cultural export

absaetze.t: On a tour of ceramics displays in museums across Europe ahead of a landmark new Delftware exhibition she was organising, Suzanne Lambooy realised they all had something in common: they were empty of people. “There was no one there because ceramics can feel cold and distanced,” she says. “They can be hard to bring alive, because the makers are anonymous, and [the objects are] often displayed in glass cases.”

But for Lambooy, ceramics are all about human connection, and she was determined to do something different. The result, Blue Loves You: The Magic of Delftware, opens this month at the Kunstmuseum in The Hague, where she is the curator of decorative arts. It will, she says, be “the biggest and most comprehensive Delftware exhibition ever”. Equally importantly, she promises it will be captivating and enjoyable.

“Delftware is so much fun, and we’re going to prove that,” she says. “We want to show the love craftspeople put into these pieces. It has inspired, and it continues to inspire, so many craftmakers—we’ll give them a platform.”

Around 1,000 objects, including vases, teapots, plates, wall plaques and tiles, will be on display at the Kunstmuseum, which has one of the largest collections of the art form that is perhaps the best-known cultural export of the Netherlands. Also on show in Blue Loves You will be Delftware-inspired pieces, including the blue dress worn by Queen Máxima of the Netherlands for her husband’s 2013 investiture, its bodice embroidered with Delft-derived flowers. “There’s a lot more to it than blue and white fridge magnets,” Lambooy says.

Although the porcelain is known for its characteristic colouring, the show will include examples of both white and multicoloured Delftware. It will explore its history, dating back to the 17th century. The form was originally a high-end Chinese import, displayed in the wealthiest homes. But when factories started to make their own version of it in Delft, it was transformed.

“It became an on-trend, functional brand that was affordable for every home and on every budget: it was the Ikea of its day,” says Lambooy, whose co-curator for the long-term show is the television presenter Janny van der Heijden (who is also a judge on the country’s version of The Great British Bake Off).

The quintessential Delftware piece was the tulip pyramid, some of the best examples of which were made for King William III, born in The Hague, and his English wife Queen Mary II, who were the joint monarchs of England, Scotland and Ireland in the late 17th century. “Mary exported Delftware to Britain—she was the most important woman in its history,” Lambooy says.

The porcelain’s connections to Dutch colonialism will also be explored, with exhibits including an installation of sugar flowers by the floral artist Natasja Sadi, whose family are originally from the former Dutch colony of Suriname and whose ancestors were enslaved.
• Blue Loves You: The Magic of Delftware, Kunstmuseum, The Hague, 28 November-31 December 2029

items.titel: Five key projects by Dezeen Awards emerging architect of the year Kuma&Elsa
items.anriss: This year Kuma&Elsa was named emerging architect of the year at the Dezeen Awards . Here, they select five projects that demonstrate the ethos of the studio.

absaetze.t: This year Kuma&Elsa was named emerging architect of the year at the Dezeen Awards. Here, they select five projects that demonstrate the ethos of the studio.
Led by Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French-Spanish urban designer Elsa Escobedo, Kuma&Elsa has completed a wide variety of projects from their bases in France and Japan.
“We believe it is important not to impose a common consistency across our projects,” Kuma told Dezeen.

“Every project is unique, shaped by a one-off combination of site and client. Preserving that uniqueness requires an open mind. Personally, I quickly lose interest when things are planned in advance.”

“That said, there are certain topics, many of which are shared by our generation, such as feminism, the care for natural resources and a shared public space, that interest us on a personal level, and I imagine they find their way into our work,” added Escobedo.
“We try to approach them with a sense of joy.”

Although they have already designed a wide range of projects, from installations to houses and public toilets, the duo would like to work on more varied schemes and unusual projects, along with completing their own, long-running renovation.
“It would be nice to actually finish this self-renovation project at some point…” said Escobedo.
“More seriously, I’d love to experiment with the reuse of materials on a larger scale, or in a European context, working with European craftspeople.”

“I would love to work on overlooked building types and uses, especially those that have little place in architectural history and attract few expectations,” added Kuma. “Designing a toilet pavilion for the Expo, a building type that nobody expects to become architecture, is one example.”
Along with the variety in projects, both architects agreed that the wide range of daily activities is what they most enjoy about being an architect.
“The variety, the diversity,” said Escobedo, when asked about her favourite part about being an architect.

“One day you’re on a construction site with incredible Japanese carpenters, the next you’re discussing a detail with your favourite thermal engineer, the following week you’re taking part in a conversation with colleagues you admire, before finding yourself struggling to install the plumbing and tiles in a shower because you had the brilliant idea of taking on a self-build project.”
Kuma also added that he enjoys the intensity of working on site.

“The construction site,” he said. “Nothing is more stressful or demanding, with all the struggles involving people and money. Yet every time I see a building taking shape, I feel glad I chose architecture. There is something addictive about it.”
Read on to find out five key projects by Dezeen Award-winning studio Kuma&Elsa, as described by the duo:
Nakano House, Tokyo, Japan, 2026

“The client’s childhood home, a traditional Japanese house, has an engawa gallery open to the garden. The new residence occupies the top two floors of a building owned by the client. She, along with her two sons and their families, will move into three apartments located on the sixth and seventh floors.

“At the centre of each apartment, we inserted a hut-like volume that gathers the quieter rooms: a small living room and the bedrooms. In the space carved out around it emerges an intermediate zone – an engawa that serves both as a place to stay and as a passage.

“Balcony, engawa, and hut thus form three spatial layers that resonate with the childhood home. The structure consists of Y-shaped modules made of lightweight steel sections and bracing cables, typically used in shelving systems.

“These modules are arranged two by two in mirrored pairs along a regular grid, with occasional inversions. From these new dwellings, one can look down across the street at the engawa of the childhood home. This project does not seek to nostalgically replicate that memory-laden place, but rather to build a new home nourished by the memories of the old one.”
One Water, Osaka, Japan, 2025

“One water is a bathing and rest pavilion for the Osaka World Expo 2025. Toilets are at first glance a pragmatic facility, dedicated to human physiology. But they are also intimately linked to contemporary issues such as the use of natural resources and gender.
“One water uses the path of rainfall on the accessible roof and its subsequent accumulation to create encounters between water and the public, and contribute to the supply of the toilets.
“The design of the pavilion allows for the reuse of materials and structural components, and makes no gender distinction in the toilets, because, after all, ‘we are all fish in one water’.”
House by the temple, Saitama Prefecture, Japan, 2024

“The house is opposite the entrance of a temple that is surrounded by a park of ancient trees and a wall, as if it belongs to another world. Reflecting this closed composition, we designed the house as an everyday world for a family.

“The main building is located at the back of the plot and has a quarter-circle plan to reduce its own shadow. The street facade is a single-storey hut, which creates a continuity between the open space of the park and the garden of the house.
“On the ground floor, the park is the backdrop to the house. On the first floor, each room offers distant views of the temple, like an observatory.”
Yamada House, Fukuoka, Japan, 2020
“A daily public space in a residential area. We create a plaza in a small residential area where human life is still at human scale.

“The house is like the background that forms the square. The composition consists of various couples: the smooth black mortar of the outer wall and the rough crushed black basalt ground, the emerald entrance hut and the crape myrtle tree with white flowers, the interior spaces and the outside square.”
Water Flower Courtyard, Montpellier, France, 2019

“The life of a flower is short: we wanted to express the fragility of a concentrated life from flowering to dispersal. This project was open to the public for a week during the Montpellier architecture festival Festival des Architectures Vives in June 2019.
“Eighteen lightweight units made of two-millimetre-thick aluminium sheets are laid out together as a forest.

“The tube is a vase that contains water and peony flowers, the bowl contains water and slate stones. All structures are self-supporting and their stability works as in a roly-poly toy. After a few days, petals start falling on the surface of the water.”
